newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians protest against plant closures.
newsitem.headline: Romanians protest against plant closures.

text.p: Thousands of Romanians poured onto the streets or blocked rail lines on Friday to protest against the centrist government's plans to close their loss-making factories in the latest phase of market reforms.

The mainly peaceful protests erupted throughout the country of 22 million a day after Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea announced a list of 17 plants with chronic losses to be closed down rapidly at the urging of the International Monetary Fund.
Media reports said the largest demonstration was in the town of Ploiesti, 60 km (35 miles) north of Bucharest, by employees of two of three oil refineries slated for closure.

The independent Mediafax news agency said 4,000 employees of the Petrotel refinery had massed peacefully outside the town hall and were refusing to disperse until they were granted a meeting with government representatives.

A further 800 workers from the Vega refinery were on their way to the protest. The oil industry, with huge excess capacity from the communist era, has been singled out as one of the country's most inefficient sectors.
The chairman of the state-run SNCFR rail authority told national radio protesters were blocking lines linking Bucharest and the eastern Moldova region.
One train was blocked at Valea Calugareasca, site of a chemical plant earmarked for closure. Police had so far taken no action and other trains were being rerouted.
The state Rompres news agency said 3,000 workers from a machine plant in the Danube River port of Braila had pushed trucks and other equipment in front of the city hall.
In Cluj, in the heart of the central Transylvania region, 1,200 workers said they would remain in their metal plant until they received more information about its inclusion on the list.
Government spokesmen offered no comment on the protests.

Ciorbea, speaking on Thursday at the end of a month-long IMF assessment of reforms, said water, power and other services would be cut to the plants due to be closed. But a spokesman for the state power utility said he had received no such order, at least for the oil refineries on the list.

The government, which launched reforms after defeating leftists in last year's elections, won IMF praise for improved results on inflation, including a record low monthly rate of 0.7 percent for July, currency stability and foreign reserves. But Ciorbea admitted that closures of inefficient industries could no longer be delayed.
